passage:
At sixteen, Himani sent her friend Zubin, 'wow, so brave of you to wear that shirt.' She meant it as a joke. Zubin's reply was one word: 'ok.' She stared at it, then typed, 'That was teasing, I love the shirt 😅' and, when he did not reply, rang him. He answered on the second ring. 'I did think you were being rude,' Zubin admitted. They laughed.

At twenty-five, Yusuf sent a 👍 to a team member from an older generation to confirm a plan. A minute later came a stiff reply: 'Was that a yes or a no?' Among Yusuf's friends a thumbs-up meant fine, but to her it looked curt, even sarcastic. Yusuf phoned. 'Sorry, it meant I'm on board.' After that he ended messages to her with a short line in words. He also learned that in some countries the same gesture is rude, so he asked his overseas colleagues how they read it.

qa.q: What did Himani do when Zubin answered with one word?
qa.a: She explained that she was teasing and then rang him.

qa.q: How do the two scenes show that missing face and voice can change a message's meaning?
qa.a: Himani's joke read as rude to Zubin, and Yusuf's thumbs-up read as curt to a colleague. A call and a line in words fixed both, and Yusuf learned that pictures and gestures carry different meanings across ages and cultures.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he answered with just 'ok'?
qa.a: Hurt or put off, because he thought the message was rude.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do when writing to colleagues in other countries?
qa.a: Check the intent, ask how an emoji is read there, or add a plain sentence to avoid offence.

grounding: Misread tone in a joking message at sixteen and differing emoji meanings across generations and cultures at twenty-five.
